title: The 2 a.m. Phone Call: How NRIs Are Navigating the Impossible Maths of Caring for Parents From Abroad
excerpt: New research quantifies what the diaspora has always known — that distance from aging parents carries a measurable health cost, and that money alone cannot bridge the caregiving gap
body:
The phone call comes at 2 a.m., or during a work meeting, or in the middle of a child's birthday party. A parent has fallen. A test result has come back. The maid has quit. For millions of NRIs, the distance between their life abroad and their parents' life in India collapses into a single, panicked moment — and then stretches back into the slow, grinding guilt of not being there.

A growing body of research is now documenting what the Indian diaspora has long felt in their bones: the collision between deeply held caregiving traditions and the practical impossibility of honouring them from 8,000 miles away. A 2025 study published in *BMC Geriatrics*, based on a cross-sectional survey in West Bengal, found that parents of migrant sons face significantly poorer health outcomes than those whose children remained nearby. Around 18 per cent of parents with migrant sons rated their health as poor, and nearly 70 per cent reported chronic ailments — compared to 57 per cent among parents of non-migrants. Psychological distress and loneliness were markedly higher, and family support for daily activities dropped sharply when sons had moved away.

The study confirms what eldercare professionals across India have been observing for years. "NRI patrons are usually on the other side of the clock," says Dr. Poulomi Bhattacharya, founder of SilverGenie, an elderly care service provider. "Trust, peace of mind, and preparedness are of the highest importance to them."

## The Cultural Weight

In most Indian families, caring for aging parents is not a logistical question — it is a moral one. The expectation, deeply embedded in Hindu, Muslim, and Sikh traditions alike, is that children — particularly sons — will provide for their parents in old age. Moving abroad does not erase that expectation; it merely makes fulfilling it exponentially harder.

A separate study from Springer Nature found that financial remittances from migrant children improved older parents' self-rated health by a factor of 1.65 and reduced depression by 55 per cent. But money, the researchers concluded, "cannot fully compensate for caregiving needs." The presence of a child — someone to accompany a parent to the doctor, to notice a change in appetite, to simply sit in the same room — remains irreplaceable.

For NRIs, this creates what researchers call a "transnational care gap." You can wire money instantly. You can order groceries on BigBasket. You cannot hold your mother's hand during a chemotherapy session from Houston.

## The Rise of Eldercare-as-a-Service

The gap has spawned an entire industry. Companies like Emoha Eldercare, SilverGenie, Samarth, and PHE Healthcare now offer what amounts to outsourced filial piety: round-the-clock attendants, medical coordination, hospital accompaniment, remote monitoring, and even social engagement programmes to combat loneliness. The cost ranges from Rs 6,000 to Rs 45,000 per month, depending on the level of service.

Devna Kumar, an NRI in Sydney, turned to Emoha when her father suffered a brain bleed and she could not extend her stay beyond a month. "When you're outside India, it's not possible to fly down frequently," she told Livemint. "But I wanted to stay informed about the outcomes of the doctor visits and also monitor the nurses." She pays Rs 36,000 monthly for a full-time attendant plus an annual subscription for doctor visits and a dedicated point of contact.

Niharika, a US resident whose mother has Parkinson's disease, uses PHE Healthcare as the "quarterback" for all her mother's needs. "Since the doctor, nurse, caretakers, my brother and I all receive daily updates, no time is lost in catching people up. We are able to move at speed and alignment when decisions are to be made."

The 60plus India community platform reports that "almost 99 per cent of our customers are parents of NRI kids." The pattern is consistent: the child abroad initiates the service, not the parent in India.

## The Guilt That Stays

What no service can fully address is the emotional toll. Indian culture does not have a vocabulary for "I hired someone to take care of my parents because I live in another country." The closest approximation carries an undertone of failure. NRIs describe a persistent, low-grade guilt — sharpened by every WhatsApp call where a parent sounds weaker, every festival spent apart, every cousin's pointed remark about who is "really there."

A study on South Asian families in the US and India found that 76 per cent of Asian Indian female caregivers were employed outside the home, creating compounding role conflict even for those who had not emigrated. For those abroad, the conflict is existential: the career that took you overseas is the same career that keeps you from the bedside.

India's UNFPA Ageing Report 2023 noted that the country's elderly population is growing rapidly with insufficient infrastructure to support it. The Economic Survey has flagged eldercare as a looming crisis. With 140 million seniors and rising healthcare costs, the system that once relied on joint families and sons who stayed close is buckling under the weight of a globalised workforce.

## What Can Be Done

Practical solutions are emerging. Remote monitoring systems, culturally adapted for Indian households, are being developed. Eldercare startups are expanding into tier-2 and tier-3 cities. Some NRIs are forming informal networks — WhatsApp groups of diaspora members in the same city whose parents live in the same neighbourhood in India, coordinating check-ins and emergency response.

But the deeper question remains unanswered: how does a culture built on physical presence adapt to a generation defined by physical absence? The answer, for now, is imperfectly — with money, with technology, with hired hands, and with the quiet hope that it is enough. For most NRIs, it never quite feels like it is.
